itihasa_bhagavad_gita_chapter2_verse55.introduction: Bhagavad Gita Chapter 2 Verse 55 is situated within the sacred unfolding of the Bhagavad Gita, where narrative history and spiritual instruction are presented as living dharma rather than distant mythology. The scene arises amid complex human relationships, duties to family and kingdom, and the tension between personal emotion and cosmic order. Elders, seekers, warriors, and sages become participants in a moral universe in which every action carries both visible and subtle consequences. The traditional telling preserves memory of lineage, vows, pilgrimage spaces, and divine intervention, allowing the listener to see how Sanatana Dharma is practiced in difficult circumstances rather than in abstraction alone. This section should be approached as both sacred literature and ethical guidance: it teaches how intention, discipline, and reverence shape conduct. The narrative focus here is a precise spiritual instruction delivered in the battlefield dialogue of Kurukṣetra. By reflecting on character motives, setting, and dialogue, the reader enters the contemplative method of itihasa study, where historical remembrance supports inner refinement and devotion.

verse.sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
प्रजहाति यदा कामान्सर्वान्पार्थ मनोगतान् |
आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ||२-५५||
verse.transliteration:
śrībhagavānuvāca .
prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān .
ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate ||2-55||
verse.translation: 2.55 The Blessed Lord said  When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then is he said to be one of steady wisdom.

itihasa_bhagavad_gita_chapter2_verse55.philosophical_explanation: Bhagavad Gita Chapter 2 Verse 55 offers a layered teaching on disciplined action, inner clarity, and God-centered wisdom, presenting dharma as a harmonizing principle that integrates duty, knowledge, devotion, and self-mastery. In Vedantic reflection, the outer event is never merely external; it mirrors the inner field of the seeker where attachment, fear, pride, compassion, and discernment contend for dominance. The text therefore asks the reader to cultivate viveka, sustained discrimination between the permanent and the impermanent, while remaining active in righteous responsibilities. It also emphasizes that true strength is not aggression but alignment with satya, ahimsa in intent, self-restraint, and surrender to the Divine will. Ethical life in Sanatana Dharma emerges through disciplined action offered without egoic possessiveness, where one performs svadharma with humility and accountability. This teaching is socially relevant because it links personal transformation with collective order: families, communities, and governance remain stable only when conduct is rooted in justice, gratitude, and reverence for truth. Spiritually, the section invites bhakti and contemplative awareness, showing that liberation-oriented living can begin within ordinary duties when the heart is purified through right understanding and service.
